newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel - no move to schedule carisoprodol.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel - no move to schedule carisoprodol.

text.p: The Food and Drug Administration's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee heard evidence Tuesday that a muscle relaxer, carisoprodol, is increasingly being abused and diverted for illegal sales, but decided not enough data was available to recommend scheduling the drug.
Carisoprodol is sold by Carter-Wallace's Wallace Labs as Soma, and generically by a number of manufacturers.
It was introduced by Wallace in 1959, and is not currently on the list of controlled products monitored by the Drug Enforcement Administration.

Kira Hutchinson of the DEA told panelists that the agency has compiled evidence that in some areas, carisoprodol is the illicit drug of choice because it is easy to get by legal or forged prescriptions, by doctor shopping or on the street.
The number of diversion cases reported to DEA almost doubled, from 144 in 1994 to 224 in 1996, Hutchinson said, adding that the true incidence is likely underreported.
The agency wants to make the drug a scheduled substance, which would restrict access, impose felony penalties on diverters and require more paperwork from health professionals.
But panel members did not feel that the data warranted scheduling.
"I would not characterize this as an emergency," said panel member Eric Strain, M.D., of the Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center.
Most committee members said they needed more analysis of the prevalence of abuse and diversion, and that other measures to control the drug could be taken before scheduling.
Panel members also want human trials to determine if carisoprodol does create physical dependence.

James Costin, M.D., vice president of research and development at Wallace Labs, said that scientific data does not support the DEA's conclusion that carisoprodol is addictive. However, due to increasing reports of abuse, the company is already investigating if carisoprodol can create dependency, Costin said. Results are due in late March.

Costin also said that over the past 27 years, the FDA has only received 421 reports of adverse drug reactions for carisoprodol. With 57 million prescriptions written during that same time, the incidence of problems is "rare by any standards," Costin said.
An FDA reviewer, however, said that an analysis of DEA and FDA databases shows that carisoprodol has the same abuse potential as diazepam, a scheduled substance best known as Valium.
Physicians argued for scheduling. Peter Staats, M.D., chief of pain medicine at Johns Hopkins University Hospital, told the panel that he believes that carisoprodol does have abuse potential.
Another physician, Michael Kaplan, said that there is an emergent problem with carisoprodol and that it should be controlled as strictly as morphine.
